summary: The note surveys chimeras and hybrid creatures across mythology, culture, modern sightings, science, art, pseudoscience, cryptid subcultures and psychology. It cites various scholars who interpret hybrids as reflections of natural phenomena, animal knowledge, human aspiration or fear. It stresses that mythical chimeras are biologically implausible and that sightings lack proof.
one_line: Overview of chimeras and hybrid creatures in myth, culture, science, art and psychology, noting biological implausibility and lack of evidence for sightings.
key_facts: Greek mythology portrays the Chimera as a fire-breathing monster with the head of a lion, the body of a goat, and the tail of a serpent, said to be an omen of storms, natural disasters, and volcanic eruptions.
Dr. Amanda Hesperus, in a paper published October 5th, 2023 in the "Journal of Mythological Studies," suggested the Chimera emerged from an attempt to interpret natural phenomena.
Egyptian lore describes Ammit as a demon with the head of a crocodile, the torso of a lion, and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus.

Professor Jamal Akil, at the International Symposium on Cultural Cryptozoology in Cairo on November 17, 2023, posited that hybrid creatures reflect a society's understanding of the animal kingdom and a desire to attribute divine or supernatural qualities to them.
Dr. Emily Rosario argued in a September 12th, 2023 lecture at the Global Folklore Conference that hybrid creatures may represent an archetype of human aspiration or fear.
On December 1st, 2023, a local newspaper in a remote town of Argentina reported a farmer claiming to have seen a beast with mismatched parts roaming his fields.
Geneticist Dr. Yvonne Ortiz, in a January 2024 study, described genetic chimeraism as an organism containing cells from two different zygotes.
The mythical chimera as an amalgamation of significantly divergent species is considered biologically implausible because of differing DNA structures and reproduction mechanics.
Art historian Mark Vargas noted on February 21st, 2024 that artists use hybrid creatures to explore transformation, the unnatural, and hybridity within humanity.
Biologist Dr. Sophie Zheng, in a critical review published March 15th, 2024, dismissed cryptozoologists' theories and emphasized the need for verifiable data.
Cryptid enthusiast subcultures on forums and social media share alleged encounters and art, often blurring the line between mythology and perceived reality.

Dr. Leonard Briggs, in a study published April 10th, 2024, linked chimeric creatures in nightmares and psychological assessments to a human tendency to grapple with the 'other' and the unknown parts of the psyche.
